analysis.one_liner: Charges a rising fee on coal, oil, and gas and sends the money back to households as quarterly dividends.
analysis.headline: Introduced by a single senator with no cosponsors, the bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would impose a fee on every ton of carbon dioxide released by burning coal, oil, and natural gas, starting at $15 per ton in 2017 and rising each year. The money would go into a fund and be paid out in equal quarterly dividends to nearly every U.S. resident, with the payments phasing out for households earning over about $100,000. It would also direct $20 billion a year in grants to communities that cannot afford to protect themselves from floods, heat waves, and storms, plus funding for home weatherization and farm conservation programs. A companion fee would be charged on imported steel, cement, aluminum, and similar goods so U.S. manufacturers are not undercut by countries with no carbon price.
analysis.who_benefits: Most U.S. residents, especially low- and middle-income households. An equal-share dividend returns more in cash than the average household pays in higher fuel and electricity costs, because wealthy households consume far more energy per person. Low-income households get the full dividend with no income test below the $100,000 phaseout, plus weatherization grants that cut their heating bills and resiliency grants for flood, storm, and heat protection in communities that cannot afford them. U.S. heavy manufacturers get border protection against imports from countries without a carbon price.

how_it_helps.text: The carbon fee is returned to eligible residents in equal quarterly payments; the dividend only begins phasing out above $100,000 of income, so lower-income households receive the full amount [S3].

The bill provides $20 billion per year for Climate Justice Resiliency Grants to state, local, tribal, and community entities for projects like flood protection, evacuation planning, air conditioning for low-income housing, and relocation planning for tribes facing erosion [S3].
It provides $1.5 billion per year for the Weatherization Assistance Program, which insulates and retrofits low-income homes to cut energy bills [S3].

It funds rural energy, soil carbon, and fertilizer-efficiency programs for farmers, and opens wholesale electricity markets to demand response so customers can be paid for reducing use during peak periods [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and importers, who pay the fee on every ton of carbon content, and households that use large amounts of fuel and electricity, since fees are partly passed through to prices. The dividend phaseout above $100,000 means high-income households pay in more than they get back. Imported steel, cement, aluminum, glass, paper, and chemicals face a matching fee at the border.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal, oil, and gas producers; high-energy-use households

drawbacks.text: The fee raises the price of gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity starting at $15 per ton in 2017 and rising to $73 per ton by 2035, then 5 percent plus inflation each year; the dividend cushions but does not fully offset costs for households that drive long distances or heat large homes, and the dividend starts only after the fund is up and running [S3].

The bill commits roughly $22 billion per year in mandatory spending without the annual appropriations process, including $20 billion for resiliency grants, $1.5 billion for weatherization, and farm and rural energy programs funded directly from the Treasury [S3].

The border fee on imported steel, aluminum, cement, glass, paper, and chemicals risks trade friction with countries that consider it a disguised tariff, and its design depends on case-by-case determinations of comparable costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most low- and middle-income households the dividend and energy-efficiency funding would more than cover the higher fuel prices, and the bill is one of the few carbon-pricing designs built around returning the money directly to the public. The serious costs are concentrated: fossil fuel producers pay the fee, and energy-intensive industries and heavy users of fuel face higher prices. The $22 billion per year in automatic spending is a real fiscal commitment made outside normal budget review.

outcome.mechanism: Bernie Sanders introduced it alone on December 10, 2015; the Senate read it twice and sent it to the Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017 [S5].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 10, 2015 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance [S5].
No further action was taken after the referral; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and energy-intensive utilities were better off because no carbon fee was ever enacted, and households avoided the near-term fuel and electricity price increases the fee would have caused.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers; heavy energy users

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it; it was his sole carbon-fee proposal in the 114th Congress.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, took no action on it; no hearing or markup was ever held.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 10, 2015 and never reported it out; the action history records nothing after the referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the partisan shape is unknown; the only public supporter was an Independent senator, and no Republican or Democrat signed on [S4].

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers
industries.note: The bill charges them $15 per ton of carbon dioxide in 2017 rising to $73 by 2035, then 5 percent plus inflation annually, on every ton extracted or imported. The fee is designed to shrink demand for their products, so their interest ran directly against the bill's public health and climate goals [S3].

industries.industry: Heavy manufacturing (steel, aluminum, cement, glass, paper, chemicals)
industries.note: A matching border fee on imports of carbon-intensive goods protects U.S. plants from undercutting by countries without a carbon price, and an import-fee fund finances industrial energy-efficiency upgrades [S3].
$1.5 billion per year for weatherization and $30 million per year for municipal efficiency block grants would create steady work insulating and retrofitting homes and public buildings [S3].

industries.industry: Renewable energy and clean power developers
industries.note: A rising carbon fee makes wind, solar, and storage more price-competitive against fossil generation, and the bill funds rural energy and biodigester projects [S3].

Utilities using coal and gas would face higher fuel costs passed to ratepayers, but the bill also gives demand response providers guaranteed access to wholesale markets on equal terms, opening a revenue channel that can lower peak prices for customers [S3].
